identityCheck: Title in text 'Prophylactic Knee Bracing in Offensive Linemen of the National Football League: A Retrospective Analysis of Usage Trends, Player Performance, and Major Knee Injury' matches the filename, which is truncated after 'player performance, a'.

paper.citation: Ackerman DR, Ptasinski AM, Edmond T, Dunleavy ML, Gallo RA. Prophylactic Knee Bracing in Offensive Linemen of the National Football League: A Retrospective Analysis of Usage Trends, Player Performance, and Major Knee Injury. Orthop J Sports Med. 2023;11(8):23259671231191767.
paper.abstract: This retrospective cohort of NFL offensive linemen from 2014 to 2020 (at least 200 regular-season offensive snaps per season) compared 154 players who wore prophylactic knee braces with 1407 who did not. Braced players had fewer major knee injuries (0.013 vs 0.049 per player, P=.04) with no cumulative difference in Pro Football Focus grades, and brace use fell from 16.3% in 2014 to 5.6% in 2020.
paper.tldr: Braced NFL offensive linemen had fewer major knee injuries over 2014-2020 with no cumulative performance difference, while brace use declined each year. This is an observational association and does not establish that bracing prevents injury.
paper.methods: Retrospective cohort of linemen with at least 200 regular-season offensive snaps; bracing status was assigned by visual review of public game images and video, and major knee injuries (those requiring missed games) came from public reports. Season PFF overall, pass-block and run-block grades were compared with unpaired t tests, and injury rates with a two-sample Z test for proportions.
paper.findings: Braced players had 2 major knee injuries (0.013 per player) and non-braced players had 69 (0.049 per player), P=.04; isolated MCL injury was the most common injury in the non-braced group. Cumulative PFF overall grades were 66.2 (braced) and 66.3 (non-braced), P=.85, but the 2015 season favored non-braced players in overall (67.9 vs 63.1, P=.03) and pass-block grades.
paper.limitations: The observational design has a large imbalance in group size (154 vs 1407) and possible selection bias, and prior knee injury history was not available. Brace type was not controlled, bracing status came from images and video rather than verified records, and injury data came from public sources that may lack mechanism and grade. Practice exposure was excluded and only starters or significant reserves were included.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff should read the result as an association in selected NFL linemen, not as evidence that bracing should be mandated. The authors note that bracing decisions were largely player-specific and that cumulative performance differences were not found.
paper.athleteDev: For offensive-line staff, cumulative PFF overall and block grades showed no performance penalty from bracing, which may inform individual discussions about brace use. The single-season 2015 difference means an individual performance effect cannot be ruled out.
paper.rtp: Does not inform return to sport: the study does not examine rehabilitation, post-injury bracing or RTS timing. It cannot be used to set RTS criteria or to decide whether a previously injured knee should be braced.
